title: The Everest album of Gordon Jenkins tunes
summary: Royal's first album as featured artist, on Everest, of Gordon Jenkins arrangements with strings, including a slow A-Train.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Uh-huh. Well, I know the people enjoy them. They certainly (inaudible).
We had fun, we had fun.

It was called Garden Jenkins presents Marshal Royal. It's a record made up mainly of Garden Jenkins' tunes. He did the scoring on them and it was done with a rhythm section and all strings. Oh, about 25 or a group of them. It was made in the New York area. Somewhere in the mid-'60s, I
Can't think of the right now, but it's a label that is no longer -- Everest Records (PHONETIC), that's the name of it. It's no longer in existence.

It was Garden Jenkins' idea. I knew nothing about it. I was out on the road and they gave a telephone call to me, said, "I'd like for you to be the featured artist on the record label called Everest," and in doing so, like to do some of his songs.

So, at that time, I didn't know as much about recording as I do now, so that meant in so many words that he wanted an album of his tunes, so he could make his ratings higher and so, I did an album of particularly all of his tunes -- of course, it was interspersed with a few other things. I did -- I was probably the first one that ever did "A-Train" as a ballad, very slow and going on. They made a few issues of it. They all sold and they didn't reissue anymore after that, because the guy went out of business. The guy was just doing it as a hobby, that had the recording company. He was originally the guy that invented the Northern Site, that they used on the American planes during World War II. So, at the end of the war, he put the fabulous thing as a plaything, he put this fabulous thing out in one of the suburbs
of New York City on Long Island and started his own recording company. So he made a few records out there and when he got tired of it, he sold it out to somebody and never heard of him anymore.

I don't know the guy. He was one of the guys that invented the Norton Bomb Site. He was a technician. He didn't know anything about music. He didn't know anything about records, nothing. All he was was a technician and he built one of the finest boards for recording for a technician to work with while recording. He was one of the innovators of the building of the boards with the eight, nine, ten, 12, 14, 16 tracks and he had this out on the edge of Long Island, one of those places out there. So, that was my first time to ever record myself.
